summary: A.R.I.D (Atmospheric and Regional Interactions in Drought) is an interactive system of drought analysis designed for the contiguous United States. Most drought indices use only precipitation as their main parameter; however, drought is significantly influenced by the ability of the atmosphere to extract water from the earth. A.R.I.D uses four parameters from NASA's FLDAS collection, including precipitation, soil moisture, actual evapotranspiration, and vapor pressure deficit (VPD), which is calculated from temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure. Each parameter is assessed relative to the baseline from 1985 to 2025 for each month separately and used to identify correlations and anomalies between the parameters. Users explore these layers on a zoomable, Google Earth-style map and click any region in the U.S. to see its historical trends. The goal is more explainable drought detection that helps citizens, communities, and farmers prepare.
details: Our project is a map that displays the variables in such a way that it shows the correlation between the variables and droughts, but also correlation between variables. It is a map depicting the United States split into separate regions. 6 main data sets can be toggled: Drought Severity, Temperature, Precipitation, Evapotranspiration, Soil Moisture, and Vapor Pressure Deficit. In addition, a slidable timeline can be used to select certain keypoints, able to be changed to a monthly or yearly trend. There is also a graph, able to show patterns, fluctuations, and comparisons over time. We aim to properly show many indicators of droughts and establish a correlation effect that can be used to both inform the audience of how separate variables are correlated and to hopefully aid existing drought indexes in an easy interactive manner. We used JavaScript for our coding. Our project blends a creative vision in our UI, developing a problem that we are familiar with in California into a more easy to view style. It transforms data into a visual creation. We added a variety of new tools to help us further analyze and show trends, tools that were previously absent from the dataset. We considered missing or inaccurate data, scope, impact, scalability, navigation, the intended audience, and future usage. We used multiple data sets to complement each other and further reinforce the accuracy of the data. Although we aimed for only the contiguous United States between 1985-2025, ARID can be scaled up to earlier dates, future dates, and can encompass a global scale, provided the data is there. We made sure that the website was easy to navigate with various info boxes and tips. This is directly applicable to the intended audience, not only scientists but also the general public. Anyone that wants to learn about and factor in variables to determine the effects on droughts can use our website. In the future, the AI analyst can include a predictor, and can be widely used to protect agriculture.
